idiom_name: zod .pick()/.strip() at runtime with Pick<T, K> types
implementation_notes: TypeScript's own Pick<T, K>/Omit<T, K> are compile-time only, so the runtime projection is done by a schema library or plain code: zod's orderSchema.pick({ id: true, reference: true }) derives the receiver's schema from the source schema and, because zod strips keys that are not in the schema by default, parsing the message is itself the content filter; Ajv achieves the same during validation (additionalProperties: false plus removeAdditional), and io-ts/valibot offer equivalent derivations. What replaces the classic filter object is the derived schema - one definition, several views - and inside a typed process a small function returning Pick<Order, "id" | "reference"> is enough. A hand-written projection is still justified for nested shapes where the schema parser cannot express the retained paths cheaply.
pitfalls: Pick/Omit erase at runtime: a producer that lies about its type still ships every field, so the projection must exist as code or as a schema parse - a type alone filters nothing.

A derived schema inherits the parent's unknown-key policy, so 'strip' only holds while the parent is not .passthrough()/.loose(); switching the parent to strict or passthrough silently changes what the receiver keeps.
parse() returns a new object, and code that keeps using the original value still holds the unfiltered data - mix the parsed view with the source and the leak reappears.

Schema-derived views are derived from the same object, so a field added to the source schema joins every view that picks '*' or that was written before the field existed; per-receiver schemas must be reviewed like any contract.
